title: Controlled Crosses and Parent Verification
objective: Preserve parent identity and prevent unintended pollen, sample, label, and generation errors during controlled crossing.
coreScience: A controlled cross is a documented transfer of pollen from a verified pollen parent to a verified seed parent while excluding unintended pollen. In Cannabis, wind-dispersed pollen, delayed pollen release, mixed tools, mislabeled clones, and overlooked male or intersexual flowers can compromise a cross. A physical bag or separate room is not sufficient unless airflow, timing, seals, handling, and later seed recovery are controlled.

Verification begins before flowering. Confirm parent IDs from permanent records and, when appropriate, genotype markers or fingerprints. Map every flowering plant, inspect for unexpected sex expression, and define pollen collection, storage, viability, and disposal methods. Pollinated branches or plants require durable cross labels tied to a cross record. Open-pollinated seed from a mixed room must not be represented as a known biparental cross.

After seed set, preserve maternal plant, branch or inflorescence position, pollination date, pollen lot, personnel, and harvest lot. Progeny testing or markers can detect some errors, but no marker panel proves complete parentage unless it is sufficiently informative for the candidate parents. Control plants and unpollinated checks help identify stray pollen. Failed identity or contamination control should downgrade the seed lot rather than be hidden by a confident name.
cultivationRelevance: Use one permanent cross ID from parent qualification through seed inventory and progeny trial. Separate breeding seed from production seed and preserve exceptions and uncertainty.
measureAndRecord: Before evaluating controlled crosses and parent verification, record the breeding population, generation, identities, and measurement context, including Cross ID, verified maternal and pollen parent IDs, genotype/identity method, flowering and isolation map. Keep definitions and identifiers stable so ancestry, family, and phenotype records remain comparable across generations.

During evaluation, track pollen lot, viability and collection date, pollination date/site, exclusion method together with the mating design, environment, developmental stage, replicate or family structure, and any selection event that could alter interpretation. Preserve raw values and rejected or missing cases rather than only the selected outcome.

At the decision point, document control plants, unexpected seed set, seed harvest lot, deviations and disposition.. State the evidence supporting advancement, note uncertainty and correlated tradeoffs, and retain enough pedigree and sample traceability to reconstruct the decision later.
misconceptions: Seed collected from a labeled female automatically has the intended father. This ignores segregation, environmental effects, sampling error, and the possibility that the observed phenotype does not transmit predictably to progeny.

A closed door prevents Cannabis pollen movement. A label, generation name, or single phenotype does not establish genetic value by itself; use family, progeny, marker, or replicated performance evidence appropriate to the trait.
One matching marker proves parentage. The claim should not be generalized beyond the tested population, parents, environments, and measurement methods without additional validation.
evidenceLimits: Parentage confidence depends on isolation, candidate-parent set, marker informativeness, sampling, and record integrity. Expected genetic ratios, breeding values, and response magnitudes are model- and population-dependent, so they should not be presented as guaranteed outcomes for untested parents or environments.

Evidence from markers, pedigrees, replicated phenotypes, progeny tests, and laboratory assays answers different questions. Strong release claims require the relevant evidence type, adequate sample size, traceable methods, and confirmation that the result persists in the target breeding population and environment.

knowledgeCheck: For "Controlled Crosses and Parent Verification", put the decision in operational order: what must be verified before action, what evidence must be recorded during the work, and what condition would require a hold or escalation?

A learner claims, "Seed collected from a labeled female automatically has the intended father." Use the lesson's science and evidence limits to explain why that claim is unreliable, then name one observation or measurement that could separate the competing explanations.

Applied case — Use one permanent cross ID from parent qualification through seed inventory and progeny trial. Separate breeding seed from production seed and preserve exceptions and uncertainty. Build a verification plan using the lesson's record set (Cross ID; verified maternal and pollen parent IDs; genotype/identity method; flowering and isolation map; pollen lot, viability and collection date; pollination date/site; exclusion method; control plants; unexpected seed set; seed harvest lot; deviations and disposition.). What would you compare before and after the action, and what result would make you revise the original interpretation?
